title: DELL: The Guide It Must Beat, and the Tape That Ignored It
meta_description: Dell has not reported since Sept 1 and its next date is unconfirmed. Here is the Q3 FY2027 guide it must clear, and why the tape was not listening.
content:
There is no confirmed earnings date for Dell Technologies, and any page that hands you one as fact is selling a setup that does not exist. The last reported quarter closed September 1, 2026. Dell is expected to report around November 24, 2026, and that is an estimate assembled by people outside the company, not a date Dell has confirmed. Label it every time you see it, because the gap between those two things is where fabricated analysis lives.

What did happen is this. Dell closed October 22 at $452.95, down 6.78% on the session and roughly 17.62% across about a month. None of that loss came from a Dell print, because Dell has not printed since September 1. It came from a Lam Research earnings call. Separating those two things is the entire useful job here.

What Dell actually reported on September 1

Q2 FY2027 is the most recent hard data anyone has on this company. Revenue was $46.971B, up 58% year over year. GAAP diluted EPS was $6.34. Non-GAAP diluted EPS was $7.04. That is the floor everything else gets measured against, and it is the freshest data available.

Worth sitting with the shape of that quarter rather than just its size. Fifty-eight percent growth on a base this large is a different animal from fifty-eight percent growth in a small company. When revenue moves that fast and management simultaneously guides the full year to a much higher number, the interesting question stops being whether demand exists and becomes whether the supply chain can be navigated fast enough to keep converting it. That is precisely the question that went wrong for half the sector on October 22.

The Q3 FY2027 guide Dell has to clear

This is the number that matters most, because without a date the guide is the only fixed thing in the story. Dell guided its third quarter of fiscal 2027 to:

  • Revenue of $49.0B plus or minus $500M
  • Non-GAAP EPS of $6.50 plus or minus $0.10
  • ISG revenue growing roughly 145%
  • About $19B of AI server revenue

Four line items, and they are not equally informative. Revenue and EPS are the familiar ones. The roughly 145% ISG growth figure is doing real work, because ISG is where the infrastructure build is landing. The $19B of AI server revenue in a single quarter is the number to watch most closely, and the reason has nothing to do with the current quarter: set it beside the $74.0B Dell has guided for AI-optimized server revenue across the full fiscal year and the concentration becomes obvious. A large share of one year's AI server forecast sits inside one quarter's guide. If that quarter slips, a good December does not rescue the year.

The fiscal year is the real bar

Guidance for fiscal 2027 was raised to $192B from $167B, a jump of 69%. AI-optimized server revenue goes to $74.0B. Non-GAAP EPS goes to $25.50. The raise from $167B to $192B is the single largest input in this story and the one most often skipped past.

Guidance is not a result. It is a management estimate issued on a specific day against a specific supply chain, and the October 21 Lam Research call challenged the assumption sitting underneath it. Tim Archer, the equipment maker's chief executive, said: “As we move into calendar year 2027, we see clean room space availability and supply chain constraints for certain components continuing to limit chip makers and equipment companies' ability to fully meet end demand.” His colleague was blunter about scope: “The whole industry is going to have to work through very similar things.”

Dell did not respond to those remarks, because Dell was not on the call. But Dell sells the box that constrained components eventually go into, and a comment about clean room space and component availability is a comment about Dell's ability to hit a $49.0B quarter. That inference proves nothing on its own. It is the mechanism connecting an equipment maker's remarks to a server vendor's guide, and it runs both ways.

Why no pre-earnings setup exists to run

Be plain about this. There is no confirmed date. Dell is also no longer in the live scanner universe this site tracks, which means there is no score to weigh, no days-left countdown, and no scanner reading to lean on. A pre-earnings playbook needs a date and a tape to read. This article can honestly give you neither.

What it can give you instead is a benchmark, and benchmarks do not expire. Until Dell confirms a date, the guide is fixed and the November estimate is soft, so keep them in separate columns in whatever you are tracking. If a date eventually appears on Dell's own investor relations page it becomes real. Until then it is a guess with a plausible shape, and treating a guess as a date is how an honest draft turns into a fabricated one.

Why October 22 was not an earnings reaction

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 6.72% to 10,731.98, a drop of 773.58 points and its worst single session since June 23, 2026. It also closed at its lowest level since July 29. Roughly $200 billion of market value left the index's 30 members in one afternoon. The iShares Semiconductor ETF fell 6.79% to 475.69, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF fell 5.99% to 523.35, and the S&P 500 gave up only 1.21%. This was not a broad market event with a semiconductor edge. It was a semiconductor event.

The trigger was a supply remark, not a demand one. Lam Research's chief financial officer, Doug Bettinger, said “this revenue guide would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints that we are actively managing.” The constrained revenue was roughly $300M to $400M for the quarter, with delayed shipments moving to the March quarter. Lam had reported a record quarter on October 21, growth of about 54% in the reported quarter, with a December-quarter guide near $8.6B. It fell roughly 6% after hours, then 11.76% on October 22, and roughly 25.10% over about a month.

Here is the part that matters for Dell specifically. AMD fell 8.10% on October 22 with its print five weeks away. Vertiv fell 7.81% with its print six days away. A name that had not reported fell as hard as one that had. Dell's 6.78% decline sits inside that band, on the same index, on the same day, for the same reason.

And demand was explicitly not the story. NVIDIA's chief executive Jensen Huang, speaking at GTC Berlin the same morning, described neocloud demand as “off the charts.” What repriced was the supply chain and the financing built around it: Meta running near-zero free cash flow, Alphabet carrying historically negative free cash flow from its AI buildout, and strain in neocloud funding, with CoreWeave down 10% and sitting about 39% below its early-October level. There was a macro overlay too, with Brent crude pushed above $110 a barrel after an attack on a Saudi oil facility. The tape was not listening to Dell. Dell said nothing.

How to track the guide without a date

Concrete next steps, in order:

  1. Treat November 24 as an estimate until Dell's investor relations page says otherwise. Do not let a third-party calendar promote it into a confirmed date.
  2. Hold the Q3 FY2027 guide as the fixed benchmark: $49.0B plus or minus $500M of revenue, $6.50 plus or minus $0.10 of non-GAAP EPS, roughly 145% ISG growth, about $19B of AI server revenue. None of those move until management moves them.
  3. Judge every single-day move in Dell against the semiconductor index, never in isolation. If Dell's session matches SOX, you are looking at the sector event and there is no Dell information inside the price.
  4. Track the $19B AI server line against the $74.0B full-year figure. That ratio, not a headline revenue beat, is what tells you whether fiscal 2027 at $192B is still intact.
  5. When Dell does report, grade it on both horizons at once: the $49.0B quarter and the $192B year. One is the trade, the other is the thesis, and they are allowed to disagree.

Dell lost 6.78% on a day it said nothing at all. That is the cleanest available statement of how little of this tape is about Dell. The guide sits there unchanged, waiting on a date.
